userPrompt: Can I require employees to work more than 48 hours a week in the EU?
responseText:
**No, you generally cannot require employees to work more than 48 hours per week in the EU.**

The **Working Time Directive (2003/88/EC)** applies across all EU member states and sets a hard limit:

- **Maximum average working time**: 48 hours per week, **including overtime**, calculated over a reference period (usually 4 months, sometimes up to 6 or 12 months depending on the country and sector).
- This is an **individual opt-out** regime in most countries: an employee must **freely agree** in writing to work more than 48 hours on average. The agreement must be reversible (the worker can opt back in with reasonable notice).

### Key points for employers
- You **cannot** make working >48 hours/week a condition of employment or discipline/fire someone for refusing to opt out.
- The 48-hour limit is a **health and safety** rule, not a mere contractual one. Breaches can lead to fines, liability for health claims, and enforcement by labour inspectorates.
- Some sectors (e.g. transport, healthcare, offshore work) have specific derogations or longer reference periods, but the core protections usually still apply.
- **On-call time, standby time, and rest periods** (11 consecutive hours per 24h and 24h uninterrupted rest per 7 days, or equivalent) are strictly regulated and count toward the 48-hour limit in many situations.

### National variations
Rules differ slightly by country:
- Some (e.g. France, Netherlands, Spain) make it very difficult to exceed 48 hours regularly.
- Others (e.g. UK — post-Brexit but still similar, Germany, Poland) allow individual opt-outs more readily, but the employer must keep detailed records and respect the worker’s right to withdraw.
- Several countries cap the absolute maximum at 56–60 hours in any single week even with an opt-out.

**Recommendation**: Never assume a blanket “yes”. Require case-by-case written opt-outs, maintain accurate records of all working time (including emails and messages outside normal hours), and consult local employment counsel for the specific member state(s) involved. Systematic pressure to work over 48 hours can invalidate opt-outs and expose the company to significant risk.
